steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper describing the design and first usability evaluation of RehabCoach, a chatbot app meant to support unsupervised upper limb therapy after stroke. Motivate unsupervised therapy and its problems, introduce the app and the platform it builds on, and state the goals of the study.

- RehabCoach: a chatbot app built on MobileCoach

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
People after a stroke often do not fully recover their upper limb function, and this has a negative impact on independence and quality of life. Increasing the dose of upper limb therapy (i.e., task repetitions and therapy time) may improve functional outcomes, or prevent losing in the long term the improvements gained in the early rehabilitation phase. However, the current rehabilitation model is mainly based on one-to-one therapy sessions, and with the limited resources that are available (e.g., low therapist-to-patient ratio) it is hard to increase therapy dose.

Unsupervised therapy, which means patients training without any direct external supervision, could be a way to increase dose without putting more strain on the healthcare system. Especially at home, unsupervised therapy could help to rely less on hospital stays and visits, so that access to rehabilitation services is ensured even when the healthcare system is under pressure, like during the COVID-19 pandemic. Also, studies have shown that unsupervised therapy can be comparable to standard care.

In the literature there are many tools that may support unsupervised therapy, such as booklets of exercises, virtual reality systems, and actuated robots. But unsupervised therapy has important challenges, like low engagement and motivation to train, poor adherence to the therapy schedule, and lack of social interaction and of feedback on progress. Some attempts to address these challenges are weekly communication with a therapist or multiuser therapy exercises, and these can increase adherence but they depend on external persons being present. A gaming environment in rehabilitation may also increase motivation, but it does not solve the problem of lack of social interaction.

- RehabCoach
  - digital interventions may address gaps (cite)
  - novel chatbot-based mobile app, complements existing unsupervised therapy methods
  - based on MobileCoach (cite): open-source platform for health interventions; personal relationship user-digital coach via chat; long-term compliance (cite)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
People after a stroke often do not fully recover their upper limb function, and this has a negative impact on independence and quality of life. Increasing the dose of upper limb therapy (i.e., task repetitions and therapy time) may improve functional outcomes, or prevent losing in the long term the improvements gained in the early rehabilitation phase. However, the current rehabilitation model is mainly based on one-to-one therapy sessions, and with the limited resources that are available (e.g., low therapist-to-patient ratio) it is hard to increase therapy dose.

Unsupervised therapy, which means patients training without any direct external supervision, could be a way to increase dose without putting more strain on the healthcare system. Especially at home, unsupervised therapy could help to rely less on hospital stays and visits, so that access to rehabilitation services is ensured even when the healthcare system is under pressure, like during the COVID-19 pandemic. Also, studies have shown that unsupervised therapy can be comparable to standard care.

In the literature there are many tools that may support unsupervised therapy, such as booklets of exercises, virtual reality systems, and actuated robots. But unsupervised therapy has important challenges, like low engagement and motivation to train, poor adherence to the therapy schedule, and lack of social interaction and of feedback on progress. Some attempts to address these challenges are weekly communication with a therapist or multiuser therapy exercises, and these can increase adherence but they depend on external persons being present. A gaming environment in rehabilitation may also increase motivation, but it does not solve the problem of lack of social interaction.

Digital interventions may play a key role in addressing these gaps. To explore this, we propose RehabCoach, a novel chatbot-based mobile application that is designed to complement and support existing methods for unsupervised therapy. RehabCoach is based on the MobileCoach framework, which is an open-source platform for health interventions. MobileCoach relies on building a personal relationship between the user and a digital coach, mainly through a chat function, to promote long-term compliance with the intervention. RehabCoach does not deliver therapy directly. It uses MobileCoach's digital coaching system, for example to send messages that encourage patients to adhere to predefined therapy plans or to give feedback, instead of just conventional reminders. MobileCoach-based interventions were already applied and validated in different populations and applications, but never in people after stroke, who might have additional challenges with using digital tools.

In the long term we want to use the RehabCoach app together with one or more robotic devices, to increase patients' adherence and motivation to train unsupervised (in the clinic or at home). As a first step, we developed a first version of RehabCoach that we presented to primary (i.e., stroke patients) and secondary (i.e., healthcare professionals) users in a single evaluation session. This first version is not connected to a rehabilitation device yet, but it still lets users get involved early, in a first iteration of the app design, so that we can collect data and feedback on usability for the next version and promote acceptance in the future. Also, testing the app separately from a robotic device means patients are not introduced to many different technologies at once, and this limits possible confounding factors when evaluating usability.

In this paper we describe the interdisciplinary development and the preliminary usability assessment of RehabCoach. The primary goal is to assess if individuals after a stroke can successfully interact with this kind of digital tool after minimal instructions. The secondary goal is to collect quantitative and qualitative feedback on the usability of RehabCoach and suggestions for improvements from primary and secondary users, which could help drive the design of future digital interventions that support rehabilitation after stroke.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
People after a stroke often do not fully recover upper limb function [1], which negatively impacts their independence and quality of life. Increasing the dose (i.e., task repetitions and therapy time) of upper limb therapy may enhance functional outcomes or prevent the long-term loss of improvements gained during the early rehabilitation phase [2,3]. However, the current rehabilitation model, mainly based on one-to-one therapy sessions, together with the limited resources available (e.g., low therapist-to-patient ratio [4]), makes increasing therapy dose challenging.

Unsupervised therapy, defined as patients training without any direct external supervision, might be a way to increase dose without further straining the healthcare system. Especially when applied at home, unsupervised therapy could help decrease reliance on hospital stays and visits, ensuring access to rehabilitation services even when the healthcare system is under pressure, as during the COVID-19 pandemic [5,6]. Furthermore, studies have shown that unsupervised therapy can be comparable to standard care [7].

The literature describes a wide range of tools that may support unsupervised therapy, such as booklets of exercises [8], virtual reality systems [9,10], and actuated robots [11,12]. However, unsupervised therapy raises important challenges, such as low engagement and motivation to train, poor adherence to the therapy schedule, and lack of social interaction and feedback on progress [13,14,7]. Attempts to address these challenges include weekly communication with a therapist [15] or multiuser therapy exercises [9], which can increase adherence but rely on the presence of external persons. Integrating a gaming environment into rehabilitation may also increase motivation [16], but it does not solve the lack of social interaction.

Digital interventions may play a key role in addressing these gaps [17]. To explore this, we propose RehabCoach, a novel chatbot-based mobile application designed to complement and support existing methods for unsupervised therapy. RehabCoach is based on the MobileCoach framework [18,19,20], an open-source platform for health interventions that relies on establishing a personal relationship between the user and a digital coach, mainly through a chat function, to promote long-term compliance with the intervention [21]. RehabCoach is not meant to deliver therapy directly; it takes advantage of MobileCoach's digital coaching system, for instance to send messages encouraging patients to adhere to predefined therapy plans or to give feedback, rather than only implementing conventional reminders [22,23]. MobileCoach-based interventions have already been applied and validated in different populations and applications [24,25], but never in people after stroke, who might face additional challenges in using digital tools.

Our long-term vision is to use the RehabCoach app in combination with one or more robotic devices to increase patients' adherence and motivation to train unsupervised (in the clinic or at home). As an initial step, we developed a first version of RehabCoach to be presented to primary (i.e., stroke patients) and secondary (i.e., healthcare professionals) users in a single evaluation session. This first version is not yet connected to a rehabilitation device, but it still allows users to be involved early in a first iteration of the app design, so that data and feedback on usability can be collected and incorporated into the next version, promoting its future acceptance [26]. Furthermore, testing the app separately from a robotic device avoids introducing patients to many different technologies at once, limiting potential confounding factors when evaluating usability.

In this paper, we describe the interdisciplinary development and preliminary usability assessment of RehabCoach. The primary goal is to assess whether individuals after a stroke can successfully interact with such a digital tool after minimal instructions. The secondary goal is to collect quantitative and qualitative feedback on the usability of RehabCoach and gather suggestions for improvement from both primary and secondary users, which could help drive the design of future digital interventions supporting rehabilitation after stroke.
